script.opening: (Quiet, tense, rubbing his face.) "I came in on my own — my partner's at work, and honestly I wanted to hear this by myself first. The sperm test came back abnormal. Does that mean it's my fault we haven't got pregnant? Does it mean we'll never have kids? I feel like I've let her down."

facts.text: If asked how it was collected: "Not that I know of. I just did what the form said" — 3 days' abstinence, at the lab within an hour, all collected. Had a cold with a fever about 6 weeks before the test.

"I'll go through all of it with you. I just want to know what actually matters." Smokes 10 a day. Drinks about 20 units a week. BMI 31. Long hot baths most nights; laptop on his lap. If asked: used a "testosterone booster" from the gym for a few months last year — not injected steroids. No cannabis.
"Nothing I can think of" — no undescended testes, mumps, groin surgery, chemotherapy or STIs. No regular medicines. No allergies.
"No, nothing I've noticed" — no lumps, pain or heaviness. Has never checked himself.
About 14 months of regular unprotected sex. "It's become a bit of a chore, if I'm honest. We're tracking everything." Partner, Lucy, 32 — regular periods, no known problems, has had no tests yet.
"She's wanted this for ages. If it's me, then I'm the reason. I haven't told her the result yet." "I'm not sleeping great. I keep reading stuff online."
Bus driver. Sits for long shifts.

Anxious and self-blaming. Asks: "Does that make a difference to sperm?" about lifestyle. Lifted by hearing one test isn't final: "So it might be fine next time?" Ready to talk to Lucy if encouraged: "I think I need to. I just didn't know what to say." If told plainly it's his fault or that IVF is the only option, he becomes tearful and withdrawn.

ice.ideas: "It's my fault, and we'll never have kids."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt at letting Lucy down; hasn't told her; worried she'll see him differently.
ice.expectations: "Just to know if it's my fault and whether we can have kids."

cues: "I wanted to hear this by myself first." — he hasn't told his partner.
"I feel like I've let her down." — blame to address.
"A bit of a chore." — strain on the relationship.

checkpoints.text: Explains that a single abnormal semen analysis must be CONFIRMED with a REPEAT (ideally at 3 months, given the ~72-day sperm cycle; as soon as possible if grossly abnormal — NICE NG257) before drawing conclusions — avoiding catastrophic interpretation of one result

Takes a male-factor history and addresses MODIFIABLE factors (smoking, alcohol, anabolic steroids/recreational drugs, obesity, possible scrotal heat (association only), medications, occupational exposures, intercourse timing/frequency)

Arranges a face-to-face EXAMINATION with a chaperone offered (testicular volume, varicocele, absent vas, hypogonadism signs — not possible on video) and PALPATES FOR A TESTICULAR MASS — recognising subfertile men’s higher testicular-cancer risk and that NICE NG12 advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis, or direct-access ultrasound for persistent symptoms
Arranges relevant tests (FSH/LH/testosterone ± prolactin, genetic/specialist if severe) and refers to FERTILITY/andrology services now (NICE NG257: the couple already meets the 1-year criterion)
Frames fertility as a COUPLE issue — ensures his partner is assessed in parallel, and that a male abnormality does not mean the cause is solely his — referring them as a couple

Avoids false despair — explains that abnormal results do not mean "never", that optimisation may improve natural conception, and that assisted options (IVF, IVF with ICSI) exist — with realistic, honest hope

Addresses the SELF-BLAME/guilt compassionately (fertility issues are common and not a personal failing or matter of fault), manages the emotional/relationship impact, and encourages involving his partner as they face it together

Safety-nets and follows up: the repeat test and timeline, lifestyle optimisation, face-to-face examination/testicular safety-netting and any suspected cancer pathway referral, couple-based fertility referral, hormone results, and emotional support including counselling (NICE QS73; HFEA) — accurate, compassionate fertility care, not cold facts or false reassurance

worked.txt: "Before anything clinical — please hear this: this is not your fault, and you haven’t let anyone down. Fertility difficulties are really common, they’re usually nobody’s ‘fault’, and they’re often about the couple together, not one person. I’m really glad you came."

"Crucially, one sperm test doesn’t give us the full picture — the numbers vary a lot, and things like a recent illness can affect it. Sperm take about three months to be made, so we repeat the test after a few months before drawing any firm conclusions."

"There’s plenty we can work on that genuinely improves things — smoking, alcohol, weight, possibly keeping the area cool, though the evidence there is weaker, and any supplements or gym products like steroids, which really affect sperm. And I’d like to examine you in person — I can’t do that on video, so we’ll book a separate appointment, and you’re welcome to have a chaperone. It’s a good chance to check the testicles are healthy too."

"When I examine you I’ll be checking for any lumps — men with lower counts have a slightly higher chance of testicular problems, so it’s worth being thorough. If I ever found something, I’d arrange a scan or refer you quickly, but that’s being careful, not expecting it."

"Two important things: I’ll refer you both to fertility services now — after more than a year of trying you already qualify — because your partner needs checking too, and this is a team effort. And an abnormal result absolutely does NOT mean never: many couples conceive after some changes, and there are treatments like IVF and ICSI that work even with low numbers."

"This is a lot to carry, especially alone. Would it help to bring your partner next time? You’re in this together, and facing it as a couple usually helps. How are you feeling in yourself with all this?"

f.learning: An abnormal semen analysis must be interpreted and communicated carefully. A single abnormal sample should be CONFIRMED with a REPEAT before drawing conclusions — sperm parameters vary widely and are affected by recent illness/fever, abstinence period and collection — and because spermatogenesis takes about 72 days, NICE NG257 advises the repeat ideally 3 months after the first (as soon as possible if grossly abnormal/azoospermic). Take a male-factor history and address MODIFIABLE contributors (smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs — notably anabolic steroids, which suppress sperm production — obesity, medications, occupational exposures, and intercourse timing/frequency; raised scrotal temperature is associated with poorer semen quality, though benefit from looser clothing is uncertain), which can meaningfully improve borderline results. EXAMINE face to face (not on video; chaperone offered) testicular volume, varicocele, absent vas and hypogonadism signs, and — critically — PALPATE FOR A TESTICULAR MASS, because subfertile men have a somewhat increased testicular-cancer risk and NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) advises considering a suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis (and direct-access ultrasound for unexplained or persistent testicular symptoms); do not miss this while focused on fertility. Arrange hormonal tests (FSH, LH, testosterone ± prolactin; genetic/specialist tests if severe) and refer to fertility/andrology services now (NICE NG257: after 1 year of trying the couple is assessed together — at 14 months they qualify), framing fertility as a COUPLE issue — the partner must be assessed in parallel and a male abnormality does not mean the cause is solely his. Avoid false despair: abnormal results do not mean "never", many men with low counts conceive (especially after optimisation), and assisted options (IVF, and IVF with ICSI — which can fertilise with very few sperm) exist, with counselling offered (NICE QS73; HFEA Code of Practice). The hidden agenda is self-blame and guilt, with the patient choosing to hear it alone; address the blame compassionately (fertility issues are common, multifactorial and not a personal failing or matter of fault), correct the catastrophe, manage the emotional/relationship impact, encourage involving the partner, and deliver accurate information — neither cold facts nor false reassurance.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG257 Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (March 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE QS73 Fertility problems (2014, updated March 2026) · [4] HFEA Code of Practice (counselling in licensed clinics)
knowledge.summary: One abnormal semen analysis is a starting point, not a verdict. Repeat it (ideally at 3 months, sooner if the deficiency is gross), look for modifiable factors, examine the testes face to face, and refer the couple together after a year of trying. Take the self-blame seriously.

points.t: NICE NG257 [1]: if the first semen analysis is abnormal, offer a repeat confirmatory test, ideally 3 months after the first so a full cycle of sperm production can pass, or as soon as possible if there is a gross deficiency (azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia). Recent fever, the abstinence interval and collection problems can all lower a single result.

NG257 [1]: couples who have not conceived after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse should be offered clinical assessment and investigation together. Refer earlier, at presentation, if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factor. At about 14 months with an abnormal result, this couple qualifies now.

Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, anabolic steroids or testosterone (which suppress sperm production), raised BMI, some prescribed drugs and occupational exposures can all reduce semen quality. Elevated scrotal temperature is associated with poorer semen quality, though it is uncertain whether looser clothing improves fertility [1].

This needs a face-to-face appointment: testicular volume and consistency, a palpable varicocele, presence of both vasa, and signs of androgen deficiency. NG257 [1]: for a clinically detected varicocele with abnormal semen, consider radiological or surgical treatment, taking female fertility factors into account.

Men with impaired semen quality carry a somewhat higher risk of testicular cancer, so examine rather than assume. NICE NG12 [3]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis, and consider direct-access ultrasound for unexplained or persistent testicular symptoms.

Hormones (FSH, LH, testosterone, with prolactin if indicated) guide the specialist, particularly when the count is very low. Genetic tests (karyotype, cystic fibrosis screen, Y-chromosome microdeletions) are specialist decisions for severe oligozoospermia, azoospermia or an absent vas.

Assess both partners in parallel. A male-factor result does not rule out a female factor, and treatment is planned for the couple. Options range from lifestyle change and treating a cause through to IVF with ICSI, which needs only a small number of sperm.

NICE QS73 [2]: people having fertility investigations and treatment should be offered counselling before, during and after, and licensed clinics must offer it (HFEA [4]). Guilt, low mood and strain on the relationship are common and worth asking about directly.

dg.d: Let him say what he fears first: fault, never having children, letting his partner down, and wanting to hear it alone.
Relationship, whether his partner knows, stress of timed intercourse, sleep and mood, work exposures.
Face-to-face examination: testicular volume and consistency, varicocele, vasa, androgen signs. Repeat semen analysis (ideally at 3 months), FSH, LH, testosterone ± prolactin.
Confounders in a single sample; modifiable factors; varicocele; hormonal or genetic causes; female factor still possible.
Asked about testicular lumps or change; planned examination; knew the NICE NG12 route for a non-painful testicular change.
Explained a single abnormal result needing confirmation, without catastrophe or false reassurance.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Couple referral now (over 1 year trying, NG257), repeat test, hormones, face-to-face exam, counselling offered.
Smoking, alcohol, drugs, anabolic steroids, weight, medicines and heat addressed as shared, practical steps.
Testicular and mood safety-net; exam booked; results review; plan for the partner’s own assessment.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “my fault” and “let her down”, and the stress of “tracking everything”, and explored them.
Idea (his fault), concern (permanent infertility, letting her down), expectation (to know if children are possible).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — guilt at letting Lucy down; hasn't told her; worried she'll see him differently — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Tom, it’s Dr Shah. Thanks for joining the video call. I can see you’ve had your semen test result — before I say anything, tell me what you’ve been told and how you’re feeling.
model.why: Starts with his understanding and emotion

model.text: I came on my own. My partner’s at work, and honestly I wanted to hear this by myself first. It says abnormal. Is it my fault we haven’t got pregnant? Does it mean we’ll never have kids? I feel like I’ve let her down.

That’s a lot to be carrying, and I’m really glad you came. Let me say one thing straight away: this is not about fault, and one test doesn’t tell us you’ll never have children. I’d like to go through what the result shows, ask a few questions, and then plan the next steps together. Is that alright?
model.why: Addresses the blame early and agrees an agenda

model.text: Yeah. Okay.

The result shows a lower sperm count than expected and the sperm aren’t moving as well as usual. Was there anything around the time of the sample — a fever or illness in the months before, or a very short or very long gap since you last ejaculated?
model.why: Checks factors that make a single sample unreliable

model.text: Not that I know of. I just did what the form said.
That’s helpful. Now some questions about general health. Do you smoke, and how much do you drink in a typical week?
Does that make a difference to sperm?

It really is, because these are things that can improve the result, and that’s good news. There’s no judgement. Have you ever used anything from the gym — protein is fine, I mean steroids, testosterone or similar products?
model.why: Explains why and asks non-judgementally about anabolic steroids

model.text: I’ll go through all of it with you. I just want to know what actually matters.

Thank you. I’ll give you the list of what matters so you can look at it with your partner: smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, any gym products, weight, regular medicines, and exposure to heat or chemicals at work. Any prescribed medicines or operations down below, like surgery for an undescended testicle or a hernia?
model.why: Covers drugs, surgical history and occupational exposures

model.text: Nothing I can think of.
Any lumps, swelling or change in the feel of your testicles, or an ache there?
No, nothing I’ve noticed.
And how often are you and your partner able to have sex — has trying to time it become stressful?
model.why: Explores frequency and the pressure of timed intercourse

model.text: It’s become a bit of a chore, if I’m honest. We’re tracking everything.
You said you feel you’ve let her down. Can you tell me more about that?
She’s wanted this for ages. If it’s me, then I’m the reason. I haven’t told her the result yet.
That makes sense of why you came alone. How are you coping in yourself — sleep, mood, work?
I’m not sleeping great. I keep reading stuff online.
What were you hoping to take away from today?
Just to know if it’s my fault and whether we can have kids.

Here’s the honest picture. Sperm results vary a lot from one sample to the next. It takes about three months to make new sperm, so we repeat the test, usually after about three months, before drawing any conclusions. Many men with a low count do father children, and there are treatments, including IVF with a technique that needs only a small number of sperm.
model.why: Explains the need for a repeat and gives realistic hope

model.text: So it might be fine next time?

It might be better, or it might confirm a problem. Either way, it’s a couple question, not a blame question. Fertility checks look at both of you, and one abnormal result in you doesn’t mean there isn’t something to check for your partner too.
model.why: Frames fertility as a couple issue without false reassurance

model.text: Because you’ve been trying for over a year, you both qualify for fertility assessment now. I’d like to refer you together, arrange the repeat semen test, and do blood tests for your hormones. Your partner will need her own checks through her GP. How would you feel about telling her?
model.why: Couple-based referral, repeat test and hormones; involves partner

model.text: I think I need to. I just didn’t know what to say.

You could say it’s a first test that needs repeating, that it’s nobody’s fault, and that you’re being referred as a couple. You’re both welcome at the next appointment. Fertility clinics also offer counselling, and I can point you to support in the meantime.
model.why: Helps him plan the conversation and offers counselling

model.text: I also need to examine you in person, which I can’t do on video. It’s a quick check of the testicles for size, any swollen veins called a varicocele, and any lump. Men with lower counts have a slightly higher chance of testicular problems, so it’s worth doing properly. Can we book that this week?
model.why: Arranges face-to-face examination including testicular check

model.text: Yeah, that’s fine.

If before then you notice a lump, swelling or change in a testicle, contact us, and we’ll see you and arrange an ultrasound. And if your mood drops or you feel you can’t cope, please tell us sooner rather than later.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed?
It’s not a final answer, repeat test in about three months, bloods, an exam this week, and a referral for both of us. And talk to her.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you for the examination and we’ll go through the blood results together.

social.t: He has not told his partner. Help him plan the conversation and invite her to future appointments; relationship strain and guilt are common in male-factor subfertility.
Poor sleep and late-night searching suggest distress. Ask about mood and point to reliable fertility support rather than forums.

legal.t: His result is his own confidential information. Encourage, but do not force, sharing with his partner; do not disclose it to her without his consent (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
NICE NG257 sets the national framework for assessment and IVF access, but local ICB criteria decide funding in practice. Avoid promising a number of funded cycles.

professional.t: A video call cannot replace a genital examination. Arrange a face-to-face appointment with a chaperone offered (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).
NICE QS73: offer counselling before, during and after investigation and treatment. HFEA-licensed clinics must offer it.

community.t: Fertility Network UK runs support services, including for men. Stop-smoking services and alcohol support can help with modifiable factors.

redFlags: Testicular lump, swelling or change in shape or texture (NICE NG12 route)
Very low count or no sperm on the report (repeat urgently and specialist tests)
psychosocial: Whether his partner knows and how the relationship is coping
ice: Idea: “It’s my fault we can’t get pregnant.”
Concern: never having children and letting his partner down
Expectation: to know if they can have children

playbook.diagnosis: “This first test shows a lower count and less movement than we’d expect. One sample isn’t enough to be sure, so we repeat it in about three months and check both of you.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A single sperm test is like one snapshot of the weather. A bad day doesn’t tell you the climate. Sperm take about three months to be made, so we take another look after that.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you feel you’ve let her down. This isn’t about fault. It’s something you’ll look into together, and there are real options.”
management.psychosocial: Help him plan how to tell his partner, invite her to the next appointment, offer counselling and check mood at follow-up.
sharedPlan: Repeat semen analysis at about 3 months (sooner if a gross deficiency)
Face-to-face examination including testes and varicocele
Refer the couple to fertility services now (over 1 year trying)
Agree realistic changes: smoking, alcohol, drugs, weight
safetyNet: Testicular lump, swelling or change: contact the practice promptly for review and ultrasound
Low mood or not coping: book sooner
Review with blood results and after the examination

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost when the result is delivered as a verdict on him. The marks are for a repeat before conclusions, a proper male-factor history, a real examination and a couple-based plan, all while taking his guilt seriously.

items.fail: Treating one abnormal sample as a diagnosis.
items.why: NICE NG257 advises a repeat, ideally at 3 months, before conclusions. A single result is affected by illness, abstinence and collection.
items.fix: “This is a first result. We repeat it in about three months before deciding anything.”

items.fail: Forgetting the testicular examination on a video call, or claiming to examine remotely.
items.why: Misses a varicocele, small testes, an absent vas or a testicular lump; NICE NG12 has a route for testicular change.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face examination with a chaperone offered and explain why it matters.

items.why: Fertility is assessed and treated as a couple (NG257). His partner may also have a factor.
items.fix: “I’ll refer you both, and your partner will have her own checks.”

items.fail: Not asking about anabolic steroids or testosterone.
items.why: A common, reversible cause of low sperm production that men rarely volunteer.
items.fix: Ask plainly and without judgement, and explain why it matters.

items.fail: Answering the clinical question but ignoring “is it my fault?”
items.why: His guilt is the hidden agenda. Ignoring it fails Relating to Others.
items.fix: Name it early: “This isn’t about fault.” Return to it when planning how to tell his partner.

items.fail: Promising a good outcome or a number of funded IVF cycles.
items.why: False reassurance; outcomes and local funding are uncertain.
items.fix: Give realistic hope: many men with low counts father children, and several options exist.

items.why: The examination, repeat test and emotional support get lost.
items.fix: Book the examination, safety-net for testicular change and low mood, and plan a results review.

Illness or fever before the sample, abstinence, smoking, alcohol, drugs, anabolic steroids, weight, medicines, testicular surgery, heat or chemical exposure, testicular lumps, sexual frequency.
Guilt, not yet told his partner, poor sleep, online reading. Ask directly how he is coping.
Repeat at about 3 months, hormones, couple referral now (over a year), face-to-face exam including testicular check, counselling, and help telling his partner.
Testicular change or low mood: contact sooner. Teach-back and booked examination.

wordPics.fail: Tells him he has a low sperm count and will probably need IVF; refers him alone; no repeat test; no examination or testicular check; ignores the guilt; lectures on lifestyle.
wordPics.pass: Explains the result needs repeating, takes a male-factor history, arranges hormones and a face-to-face examination, and refers to fertility services with his partner.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: addresses the self-blame early and warmly; frames the problem as the couple’s; gives realistic hope without promises; helps him plan how to tell his partner; offers counselling; checks mood; links the examination to testicular cancer awareness with the NICE NG12 route; uses teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Well, the problem is on your side, so it’s the male factor.”
avoid.instead: “This is the first test, it needs repeating, and fertility is always looked at as a couple.”
avoid.why: Confirms his guilt and ignores the need for a repeat and for female assessment.

avoid.instead: “There are several options depending on what the repeat test and both your checks show, and many men with a low count do father children.”
avoid.why: Premature and frightening on a single result.

avoid.dont: “Stop smoking and drinking and lose some weight.”
avoid.instead: “Some things can genuinely improve sperm quality. Which of these feels doable for you?”
avoid.why: A lecture to a man already blaming himself worsens guilt and reduces engagement.

It might be better, or it might confirm a problem. Either way, it’s a couple question, not a blame question. Fertility checks look at both of you, and one abnormal result in you doesn’t mean there isn’t something to check for your partner too.
SCA_MODELS.why: Frames fertility as a couple issue without false reassurance

SCA_MODELS.text: Because you’ve been trying for over a year, you both qualify for fertility assessment now. I’d like to refer you together, arrange the repeat semen test, and do blood tests for your hormones. Your partner will need her own checks through her GP. How would you feel about telling her?
SCA_MODELS.why: Couple-based referral, repeat test and hormones; involves partner

SCA_MODELS.text: I think I need to. I just didn’t know what to say.

You could say it’s a first test that needs repeating, that it’s nobody’s fault, and that you’re being referred as a couple. You’re both welcome at the next appointment. Fertility clinics also offer counselling, and I can point you to support in the meantime.
SCA_MODELS.why: Helps him plan the conversation and offers counselling

SCA_MODELS.text: I also need to examine you in person, which I can’t do on video. It’s a quick check of the testicles for size, any swollen veins called a varicocele, and any lump. Men with lower counts have a slightly higher chance of testicular problems, so it’s worth doing properly. Can we book that this week?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges face-to-face examination including testicular check

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, that’s fine.

If before then you notice a lump, swelling or change in a testicle, contact us, and we’ll see you and arrange an ultrasound. And if your mood drops or you feel you can’t cope, please tell us sooner rather than later.
Can you tell me in your own words what we’ve agreed?
It’s not a final answer, repeat test in about three months, bloods, an exam this week, and a referral for both of us. And talk to her.
That’s exactly it. I’ll see you for the examination and we’ll go through the blood results together.

No other history recorded in the case
SCA_STEM.recent: Semen analysis reported: low sperm count (oligozoospermia) with reduced motility. First sample.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “My sperm test came back abnormal. Is it my fault, and does it mean we’ll never have kids?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG257 Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (March 2026) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [2] NICE QS73 Fertility problems (2014, updated March 2026) · [4] HFEA Code of Practice (counselling in licensed clinics)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: One abnormal semen analysis is a starting point, not a verdict. Repeat it (ideally at 3 months, sooner if the deficiency is gross), look for modifiable factors, examine the testes face to face, and refer the couple together after a year of trying. Take the self-blame seriously.

points.t: NICE NG257 [1]: if the first semen analysis is abnormal, offer a repeat confirmatory test, ideally 3 months after the first so a full cycle of sperm production can pass, or as soon as possible if there is a gross deficiency (azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia). Recent fever, the abstinence interval and collection problems can all lower a single result.

NG257 [1]: couples who have not conceived after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse should be offered clinical assessment and investigation together. Refer earlier, at presentation, if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factor. At about 14 months with an abnormal result, this couple qualifies now.

Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, anabolic steroids or testosterone (which suppress sperm production), raised BMI, some prescribed drugs and occupational exposures can all reduce semen quality. Elevated scrotal temperature is associated with poorer semen quality, though it is uncertain whether looser clothing improves fertility [1].

This needs a face-to-face appointment: testicular volume and consistency, a palpable varicocele, presence of both vasa, and signs of androgen deficiency. NG257 [1]: for a clinically detected varicocele with abnormal semen, consider radiological or surgical treatment, taking female fertility factors into account.

Men with impaired semen quality carry a somewhat higher risk of testicular cancer, so examine rather than assume. NICE NG12 [3]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for a non-painful enlargement or change in shape or texture of the testis, and consider direct-access ultrasound for unexplained or persistent testicular symptoms.

Hormones (FSH, LH, testosterone, with prolactin if indicated) guide the specialist, particularly when the count is very low. Genetic tests (karyotype, cystic fibrosis screen, Y-chromosome microdeletions) are specialist decisions for severe oligozoospermia, azoospermia or an absent vas.

Assess both partners in parallel. A male-factor result does not rule out a female factor, and treatment is planned for the couple. Options range from lifestyle change and treating a cause through to IVF with ICSI, which needs only a small number of sperm.

NICE QS73 [2]: people having fertility investigations and treatment should be offered counselling before, during and after, and licensed clinics must offer it (HFEA [4]). Guilt, low mood and strain on the relationship are common and worth asking about directly.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let him say what he fears first: fault, never having children, letting his partner down, and wanting to hear it alone.
Relationship, whether his partner knows, stress of timed intercourse, sleep and mood, work exposures.
Picked up “my fault” and “let her down”, and the stress of “tracking everything”, and explored them.
Idea (his fault), concern (permanent infertility, letting her down), expectation (to know if children are possible).
Face-to-face examination: testicular volume and consistency, varicocele, vasa, androgen signs. Repeat semen analysis (ideally at 3 months), FSH, LH, testosterone ± prolactin.
Confounders in a single sample; modifiable factors; varicocele; hormonal or genetic causes; female factor still possible.
Asked about testicular lumps or change; planned examination; knew the NICE NG12 route for a non-painful testicular change.
Explained a single abnormal result needing confirmation, without catastrophe or false reassurance.
Couple referral now (over 1 year trying, NG257), repeat test, hormones, face-to-face exam, counselling offered.
Smoking, alcohol, drugs, anabolic steroids, weight, medicines and heat addressed as shared, practical steps.
Testicular and mood safety-net; exam booked; results review; plan for the partner’s own assessment.

social.t: He has not told his partner. Help him plan the conversation and invite her to future appointments; relationship strain and guilt are common in male-factor subfertility.
Poor sleep and late-night searching suggest distress. Ask about mood and point to reliable fertility support rather than forums.

legal.t: His result is his own confidential information. Encourage, but do not force, sharing with his partner; do not disclose it to her without his consent (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
NICE NG257 sets the national framework for assessment and IVF access, but local ICB criteria decide funding in practice. Avoid promising a number of funded cycles.

professional.t: A video call cannot replace a genital examination. Arrange a face-to-face appointment with a chaperone offered (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).
NICE QS73: offer counselling before, during and after investigation and treatment. HFEA-licensed clinics must offer it.

community.t: Fertility Network UK runs support services, including for men. Stop-smoking services and alcohol support can help with modifiable factors.

redFlags: Testicular lump, swelling or change in shape or texture (NICE NG12 route)
Very low count or no sperm on the report (repeat urgently and specialist tests)
psychosocial: Whether his partner knows and how the relationship is coping
ice: Idea: “It’s my fault we can’t get pregnant.”
Concern: never having children and letting his partner down
Expectation: to know if they can have children

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This first test shows a lower count and less movement than we’d expect. One sample isn’t enough to be sure, so we repeat it in about three months and check both of you.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A single sperm test is like one snapshot of the weather. A bad day doesn’t tell you the climate. Sperm take about three months to be made, so we take another look after that.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you feel you’ve let her down. This isn’t about fault. It’s something you’ll look into together, and there are real options.”
management.psychosocial: Help him plan how to tell his partner, invite her to the next appointment, offer counselling and check mood at follow-up.
sharedPlan: Repeat semen analysis at about 3 months (sooner if a gross deficiency)
Face-to-face examination including testes and varicocele
Refer the couple to fertility services now (over 1 year trying)
Agree realistic changes: smoking, alcohol, drugs, weight

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost when the result is delivered as a verdict on him. The marks are for a repeat before conclusions, a proper male-factor history, a real examination and a couple-based plan, all while taking his guilt seriously.

items.fail: Treating one abnormal sample as a diagnosis.
items.why: NICE NG257 advises a repeat, ideally at 3 months, before conclusions. A single result is affected by illness, abstinence and collection.
items.fix: “This is a first result. We repeat it in about three months before deciding anything.”

items.fail: Forgetting the testicular examination on a video call, or claiming to examine remotely.
items.why: Misses a varicocele, small testes, an absent vas or a testicular lump; NICE NG12 has a route for testicular change.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face examination with a chaperone offered and explain why it matters.

items.why: Fertility is assessed and treated as a couple (NG257). His partner may also have a factor.
items.fix: “I’ll refer you both, and your partner will have her own checks.”

items.fail: Not asking about anabolic steroids or testosterone.
items.why: A common, reversible cause of low sperm production that men rarely volunteer.
items.fix: Ask plainly and without judgement, and explain why it matters.

items.fail: Answering the clinical question but ignoring “is it my fault?”
items.why: His guilt is the hidden agenda. Ignoring it fails Relating to Others.
items.fix: Name it early: “This isn’t about fault.” Return to it when planning how to tell his partner.

items.fail: Promising a good outcome or a number of funded IVF cycles.
items.why: False reassurance; outcomes and local funding are uncertain.
items.fix: Give realistic hope: many men with low counts father children, and several options exist.

items.why: The examination, repeat test and emotional support get lost.
items.fix: Book the examination, safety-net for testicular change and low mood, and plan a results review.
